question: A lab's final reading, in kilojoules after a sixfold scaling, is the target number — but everything starts with two small speed readings. Two probe speeds of 4 m/s and 5 m/s are added together and the sum doubled, giving the effective speed of a test slider. That speed belongs to a slider whose mass is listed as 16000 grams. From the resulting kinetic energy, 10 J is subtracted for a friction correction, and the corrected value is converted into kilojoules. Finally, the converted energy is scaled by a factor of six to represent six repeated trials. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A crane's final reading, in kilonewtons, is wanted after converting from newtons — but the acceleration behind it is built up in stages. Two recorded acceleration values, in m/s², sum to 9 and multiply to 20; engineers keep the larger of the two. From this value, 26 m/s² is subtracted, and then 27 m/s² is added back. This net acceleration acts on a 10 kg test load hanging from the crane. The resulting force is converted into kilonewtons. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

Two probe readings of 4 m/s and 13 m/s on a wind-tunnel model are added together and the sum is multiplied by 4, giving the model's effective test speed. This speed belongs to a model aircraft whose mass is stated as 45000 grams. The tunnel's ambient humidity is a separate 38%, which is not used in this calculation. The resulting kinetic energy is then doubled, multiplied again by 11, and finally multiplied by 5. What is the final energy, in joules?

A test lab's final answer, in kilojoules after one last twelvefold scaling, is needed for the report — but the process starts with two speed candidates. Two speed values, in m/s, sum to 7 and multiply to 6; technicians keep the smaller of the two as the actual test speed. This speed belongs to a 17 kg sled. The sled's kinetic energy is scaled by 12, then scaled again by 10, and converted into kilojoules. A separate stopwatch reading of 45 seconds plays no role here. Finally, the converted energy is scaled once more by a factor of 12. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A lab's final energy reading, in joules after a last subtraction of 30 J, is wanted — but the process starts with a position trace. A slider's position on a test rig follows x(t) = 3t³ − 6t² (in meters, t in seconds); its instantaneous speed — the rate of change of position — at t = 3.0 s is recorded, in meters per second. This speed belongs to a slider whose mass is stated as 59000 grams. From the resulting kinetic energy, 28 J is added, then 4 J is added again, and finally 30 J is subtracted. What is the final energy, in joules?

At a materials testing lab, two speed values, in m/s, are found to sum to 10 and multiply to 16; the larger of the two is used as the test speed of a 25 kg impact hammer. The hammer's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules, and 25 kJ is then subtracted for absorbed deformation energy. A separate humidity sensor reads 55%, which is unrelated to this result. The corrected energy is then scaled by a factor of six. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after a twelvefold scaling, is the goal — but it starts with two speed candidates. Two speeds, in m/s, sum to 7 and multiply to 10; the larger is kept as the actual speed of a sliding block whose mass is stated as 16000 grams. The block's kinetic energy is scaled by 8, converted into kilojoules, and then reduced by 17 kJ. Finally, the corrected energy is scaled once more, by a factor of 12. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A test bench's final reading, in kilonewtons after a subtraction of 28 kN, is the goal — but it starts with a speed trace. A component's speed on the bench follows v(t) = 3t³ + t² (in m/s, t in seconds); its instantaneous acceleration — the rate of change of speed — at t = 2.0 s is recorded. This acceleration acts on a 32 kg part, producing a force that is converted into kilonewtons, then scaled by a factor of 9, and finally reduced by 28 kN. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

On a go-kart test track, the kart's acceleration follows a(t) = 5t² + 3t (in m/s², t in seconds) from a standing start; the total speed gained between t = 0 s and t = 1 s, found from the area under this graph, is the kart's speed for the next stage. This speed belongs to an 11 kg battery pack on board. The pack's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules, then scaled by a factor of 9. The track's total length is 400 m, which plays no role here. Finally, 19 kJ is added. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A conveyor system's final force reading, in newtons after a last subtraction of 25 N, is wanted — but it starts with two acceleration readings. Two acceleration readings of 7 m/s² and 3 m/s² are added and the sum multiplied by 3, giving the conveyor's effective acceleration. This acts on a 154 kg load, producing a force that is scaled by a factor of 12, reduced by 25 N, doubled, and finally reduced once more by 25 N. What is the final force, in newtons?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after a fourfold scaling, is wanted — but the process begins with two speed candidates. Two speeds, in m/s, sum to 8 and multiply to 7; the larger is kept, then 28 m/s is added to it, and 30 m/s is subtracted back. This net speed belongs to a slider whose mass is stated as 14000 grams. The slider's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules. A separate wall clock nearby reads 09:15, irrelevant to the task. Finally, the converted energy is scaled by a factor of 4. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after a subtraction of 25 kJ, is the target — but it starts with two rod lengths. Two rods measure 21 cm and 283 cm; the greatest length dividing both evenly is used as the speed, in m/s, of a slider whose mass is stated as 57000 grams. The slider's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules, then doubled, then scaled again by a factor of 8. A separate pressure reading of 12 bar plays no role in this calculation. Finally, 25 kJ is subtracted. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after one last tenfold scaling, is wanted — but it starts with two rope lengths. Two ropes measure 62 cm and 97 cm; the greatest length dividing both evenly is found, and 10 is added to that number. This total is used as the speed, in meters per second, of a 10 kg weight on a pulley test rig. The weight's kinetic energy is scaled by a factor of 12, converted into kilojoules, and finally scaled once more by a factor of 10. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

On a conveyor test rig, the belt's acceleration follows a(t) = 5t² + 5t (in m/s², t in seconds) from a standstill; the total speed gained between t = 0 s and t = 1 s, found from the area under this graph, is the belt's effective speed. This speed belongs to a component whose mass is stated as 38000 grams. The resulting kinetic energy is doubled, then increased by 13 J, then multiplied by 4, and finally converted into kilojoules. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after conversion, is wanted — but the process starts with a position trace. A cart's position on a test track follows x(t) = 3t³ − 4t² (in meters, t in seconds); its instantaneous speed at t = 1.0 s is recorded, in meters per second, and then 29 m/s is added to account for a tow assist. This total speed belongs to a cart whose mass is stated as 22000 grams. The cart's kinetic energy is scaled by a factor of 4, then reduced by 25 J, and finally converted into kilojoules. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A packaging robot's final reading, in kilojoules, is wanted after converting from joules — but it begins with an acceleration profile. The robot arm's acceleration follows a(t) = 4t² (in m/s², t in seconds) from rest; the total speed gained between t = 0 s and t = 1 s, from the area under this graph, is the arm's effective speed. This speed belongs to an 8 kg gripper. The gripper's kinetic energy is scaled by 5, scaled again by 5, and converted into kilojoules. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A roller-coaster test cart's position follows x(t) = 2t³ + t² (in meters, t in seconds); its instantaneous speed at t = 1.0 s is recorded, in meters per second. This speed belongs to a cart whose mass is stated as 23000 grams. From the resulting kinetic energy, 1 J is subtracted, the result is scaled by 5, scaled again by 9, and finally increased by 6 J. What is the final energy, in joules?

Two acceleration readings, in m/s², on a robotic arm sum to 10 and multiply to 24; engineers keep the larger of the two, then add 27 m/s² measured during a jolt. This total acceleration acts on an arm segment whose mass is stated as 30000 grams. The workshop thermometer separately reads 19°C, unrelated to this task. To the resulting force, 11 N is added, then 15 N is added again, and finally 15 N is added once more. What is the final force, in newtons?

Two cable offcuts measure 14 cm and 130 cm; the greatest length dividing both evenly is used as the acceleration, in m/s², of a machine part whose mass is stated as 96000 grams. A separate voltage reading of 230 V on the control panel is not needed here. The resulting force is converted into kilonewtons, scaled by a factor of 6, and finally increased by 17 kN. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after a last addition of 7 kJ, is wanted — but it begins with two rod lengths. Two rods measure 157 cm and 226 cm; the greatest length dividing both evenly is used as the speed, in meters per second, of a slider whose mass is stated as 9000 grams. The slider's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules, then reduced by 16 kJ, reduced again by 18 kJ, and finally increased by 7 kJ. A separate voltmeter on the bench reads 5 V, which is unrelated. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

On a forklift test rig, two acceleration readings, in m/s², sum to 6 and multiply to 8; engineers keep the larger, then triple it. This acceleration acts on a forklift part whose mass is stated as 55000 grams. The forklift's fuel gauge separately reads three-quarters full, which is unrelated. From the resulting force, 10 N is subtracted, then 13 N is added back, and finally 18 N is added once more. What is the final force, in newtons?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after a final doubling, is wanted — but it begins with two speed candidates. Two speed values, in m/s, sum to 8 and multiply to 7; the larger is kept as the speed of a 32 kg block. From the block's kinetic energy, 29 J is subtracted, and the result is converted into kilojoules. A separate stopwatch reads 47 seconds, unrelated to this task. The converted energy is then scaled by a factor of 11, and finally doubled. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A go-kart's final energy reading, in joules after a last subtraction of 7 J, is the goal — but the process starts with an acceleration profile. On the kart, acceleration follows a(t) = 5t² + 6t (in m/s², t in seconds); the speed gained between t = 1 s and t = 2 s, from the area under this graph, has 27 m/s subtracted from it, then 13 m/s added back. This net speed belongs to a 3 kg battery pack. A separate fuel gauge on the kart reads half full, unrelated to the task. The pack's kinetic energy is scaled by a factor of 10, and finally 7 J is subtracted. What is the final energy, in joules?

A lab's final energy reading, in joules after a last addition of 21 J, is wanted — but it starts with two rod lengths. Two rods measure 206 cm and 50 cm; the greatest length dividing both evenly is used as the speed, in meters per second, of a 20 kg slider. A separate pressure gauge reads 4 bar, unrelated to the task. The slider's kinetic energy is scaled by a factor of 8, increased by 11 J, and finally increased once more by 21 J. What is the final energy, in joules?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules, is wanted after one last conversion — but it starts with two speed candidates. Two speeds, in m/s, sum to 14 and multiply to 48; the larger is kept as the speed of a slider whose mass is stated as 14000 grams. From the resulting kinetic energy, 30 J is added, the total is scaled by a factor of 6, then 8 J is subtracted, and finally the figure is converted into kilojoules. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?
